lessons.title: Supplier Relationship Management in African Markets
lessons.body: Supplier relationship management, or SRM, is the discipline of deliberately managing the interface between a buying organisation and its suppliers to extract maximum long term value rather than simply chasing the lowest price on each transaction. In African markets this discipline takes on a distinctive character because supply bases are often fragmented, informal in parts, geographically dispersed, and shaped by infrastructure gaps, currency volatility, and regulatory differences across borders. A procurement professional in Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, or Johannesburg who treats every supplier as interchangeable will consistently underperform one who segments suppliers and invests relationship effort where it matters. This lesson sets out a practical framework for SRM in an African context, covering segmentation, governance, performance measurement, development, and risk. The first step is segmentation. Not every supplier deserves the same attention. A useful approach is to classify suppliers along two axes: the strategic importance of what they supply and the level of supply risk. Strategic items such as specialised machinery, critical chemicals, or exclusive distribution rights sit in the high importance high risk quadrant and demand partnership style relationships with joint planning, shared forecasts, and executive sponsorship. Routine items such as stationery or basic consumables sit in the low importance low risk quadrant and are best handled through catalogue ordering, framework agreements, and light touch administration. Bottleneck items, where spend is low but risk is high, require securing supply through buffer stock, dual sourcing, or long term commitments. Leverage items, where spend is high but risk is low, are ideal for competitive tendering and aggressive negotiation. In many African markets the bottleneck quadrant is larger than buyers expect because of import dependency, port congestion, foreign exchange shortages, and single source situations. Mapping your portfolio honestly is the foundation of everything that follows. Once segmented, establish governance. For strategic suppliers create a joint steering committee that meets quarterly with a defined agenda covering demand forecasts, quality performance, innovation pipeline, and risk. Nominate an internal supplier owner, usually a senior procurement or category manager, who is accountable for the relationship. Document a relationship charter that states mutual expectations, escalation paths, and review cadence. For bottleneck suppliers, governance is lighter but must include a named contact on both sides and a standing contingency plan. For routine suppliers, governance is embedded in the contract and the ordering system. The common failure in African procurement is that governance exists on paper but meetings are cancelled, data is not shared, and problems are discovered only when production stops. Discipline in holding the meetings and circulating minutes is what separates effective SRM from wishful thinking. Performance measurement should be simple, visible, and fair. Use a scorecard with no more than six to eight metrics. Typical metrics include on time in full delivery, quality rejection rate, responsiveness to queries, price competitiveness against market benchmarks, compliance with health safety and environmental requirements, and contribution to local content or transformation goals where relevant. Score monthly, review quarterly, and share the scorecard with the supplier before the review meeting so the conversation is about improvement rather than surprise. In African contexts, be careful that metrics do not punish suppliers for factors outside their control, such as customs delays at Mombasa or Apapa, but equally do not allow those factors to become permanent excuses. Where a supplier repeatedly fails, the scorecard provides the evidence base for a corrective action plan or eventual exit. Supplier development is where SRM creates disproportionate value in Africa. Many capable local suppliers lack the systems, certifications, or working capital to meet corporate standards. A structured development programme can change that. Start with a gap assessment against your requirements, then agree a time bound improvement plan with milestones. Support can include training in quality management, assistance with ISO certification, mentoring on costing and pricing, introductions to finance providers for invoice discounting, and predictable order commitments that give the supplier confidence to invest. Large buyers in mining, telecoms, retail, and banking have used such programmes to build local supply chains that reduce lead times, lower currency exposure, and strengthen community relations. The business case is not purely altruistic; local suppliers are often faster and cheaper once they are capable. Risk management must be continuous. Maintain a live register of supplier risks covering financial health, ownership changes, labour disputes, regulatory action, climate events, and geopolitical disruption. Monitor news and credit reports, and conduct site visits at least annually for critical suppliers. Develop contingency plans for the top ten risks, including qualified alternate suppliers, strategic stock, and design alternatives. In Africa, currency and payment risk deserve special attention. If you pay in hard currency but the supplier buys inputs locally, exchange rate movements can erode their margin and trigger quality cuts or delivery failures. Consider price adjustment clauses tied to published indices, shorter payment terms, or partial advance payment for critical suppliers. Finally, remember that relationships are personal as well as contractual. In many African business cultures, trust built through consistent fair dealing, timely payment, and respect for the supplier as a partner will do more for supply security than any clause. Pay on time. Communicate bad news early. Do not use your power to squeeze margins to the point of supplier collapse. A supplier who survives and grows with you is worth more than a short term saving. Action steps for this week: segment your top fifty suppliers by importance and risk, identify your ten strategic relationships, schedule the next quarterly review for each, and publish a simple scorecard template. SRM is not a project; it is a habit, and in African markets that habit pays compound returns.

lessons.title: Contract Management and Compliance in African Procurement
lessons.body: Contract management is the process of ensuring that what was agreed during sourcing is actually delivered during the life of the contract, and that both parties meet their legal, regulatory, and ethical obligations. In African procurement, contract management is frequently the weakest link in the chain. Buyers invest heavily in tendering and negotiation, then file the signed contract and assume performance will follow. The result is value leakage, disputes, audit findings, and damaged supplier relationships. This lesson provides a practical guide to contract management and compliance tailored to African operating realities, including weak enforcement environments, multiple regulatory regimes, and capacity constraints on both sides. Begin with contract architecture. A well drafted contract for African conditions should address scope, specifications, prices and price adjustment mechanisms, delivery terms using Incoterms, payment terms and currency, warranties, liability caps, termination rights, dispute resolution, governing law, and compliance obligations. Pay particular attention to force majeure and change of law clauses, because currency controls, import bans, tax changes, and sudden regulatory shifts are common. Define what constitutes a change and how price and schedule will be adjusted. Include a clear acceptance process with measurable criteria so that disputes about quality are resolved by evidence rather than opinion. Where the supplier is offshore, specify which documents must accompany each shipment and who bears demurrage or storage costs if clearance is delayed. Ambiguity in these areas is the source of most contract disputes in the region. Once signed, the contract must be actively administered. Assign a contract manager for every significant agreement. That person owns the contract file, the obligations register, and the performance record. Create an obligations register that lists every commitment by both parties with dates and owners. Typical buyer obligations include providing forecasts, issuing purchase orders, granting site access, approving drawings, and paying on time. Typical supplier obligations include delivering to specification, maintaining certifications, submitting reports, and complying with labour and environmental laws. Review the register monthly. Many failures attributed to suppliers are actually caused by the buyer failing to meet its own obligations, such as late approvals or delayed payments. Track milestones and deliverables against the contract schedule. Use a simple dashboard showing upcoming expiries, renewal dates, price review dates, insurance renewals, and guarantee expiry. Diarise these at least ninety days in advance. In African markets, lead times for renewal approvals can be long, and a lapse in a service contract can halt operations. For long term contracts, conduct a formal annual review covering performance, pricing, risk, and continued relevance. Markets move; a contract signed three years ago may no longer reflect current costs or technology. Build in a mechanism for benchmarking and renegotiation rather than waiting for a crisis. Compliance has several dimensions. First, legal and regulatory compliance. Ensure the supplier holds all required licences, permits, and tax registrations in the relevant jurisdiction. Verify tax clearance certificates, VAT registration, and where applicable, sector specific permits such as mining, telecommunications, or health licences. Check sanctions and debarment lists, and screen for beneficial ownership where the law requires it. Second, anti bribery and corruption compliance. Many African countries have strengthened their anti corruption laws, and multinational buyers are also subject to laws such as the UK Bribery Act and the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Contracts must include anti bribery warranties, audit rights, and termination rights for breach. Gifts, hospitality, and facilitation payments must be governed by a clear policy, and staff must be trained to recognise red flags such as unusual intermediaries, cash requests, or demands for payment to secure permits. Third, labour and human rights compliance. Require suppliers to comply with local labour law, prohibit child and forced labour, and where relevant, require adherence to codes covering wages, hours, health and safety, and freedom of association. In sectors such as agriculture, mining, and construction, conduct periodic audits, including unannounced visits, and require corrective action plans for findings. Fourth, environmental and social compliance. Depending on the sector, require environmental permits, waste management plans, and community engagement records. Increasingly, buyers must report on scope three emissions and supply chain sustainability, so supplier data collection should be built into the contract. Fifth, data protection and cyber security. Where suppliers handle personal data, include clauses on lawful processing, breach notification, and security standards, aligned with laws such as South Africa POPIA, Kenya Data Protection Act, and Nigeria Data Protection Act. Dispute resolution deserves careful thought. Litigation in some African jurisdictions can be slow and unpredictable. Consider tiered dispute resolution: negotiation between contract managers, then escalation to senior executives, then mediation, then arbitration. Choose the seat of arbitration deliberately, considering enforceability of awards under the New York Convention. Many parties choose seats such as Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, or an offshore seat depending on the counterparty and the assets involved. Keep contemporaneous records of all communications, variations, and approvals. In a dispute, documentation wins. Variations are a major source of leakage. Establish a formal variation procedure requiring written requests, impact assessment covering cost and schedule, approval by the authorised person, and contract amendment. Do not allow work to proceed on verbal instructions. Train project and operations staff to route all changes through the contract manager. Audit the variation log quarterly to detect patterns, such as repeated scope creep from one department or one supplier. Finally, close out contracts properly. Conduct a final performance review, settle all claims, recover or release guarantees, return or destroy confidential information, and capture lessons learned for future sourcing. Update the supplier scorecard and the risk register. Archive the contract file in line with retention policy. Action steps: list your active contracts above a threshold, assign a contract manager to each, build an obligations register for the top ten, diarise all renewal and price review dates, and run a compliance check on licences and tax certificates for your critical suppliers. Contract management is not glamorous, but it is where procurement value is protected or lost. In African markets, disciplined administration is a competitive advantage.

lessons.title: Strategic Sourcing and Category Management in Africa
lessons.body: Strategic sourcing is the structured process of analysing spend, understanding markets, and designing supply arrangements that deliver the best total value rather than the lowest unit price. Category management is the organisational approach that groups similar spend into categories and assigns ownership so that sourcing is proactive rather than reactive. In African procurement, these disciplines are especially valuable because markets are often opaque, data is scarce, and informal suppliers dominate some sectors. A buyer who masters strategic sourcing can unlock savings, reduce risk, and build supply chains that competitors cannot easily copy. This lesson walks through the practical steps, adapted for African conditions. The starting point is spend analysis. Collect twelve to twenty four months of transaction data from the ERP and from manual records where systems are weak. Cleanse supplier names, standardise descriptions, and classify spend using a taxonomy such as the United Nations Standard Products and Services Code or a simpler internal scheme. The output should show total spend by category, by supplier, by business unit, and by country. Expect surprises. Many African organisations discover that a large share of spend sits with a long tail of small suppliers, that the same item is bought at different prices across sites, and that some categories are far larger than anyone assumed. Present the findings to finance and operations to validate them. Without credible spend data, sourcing decisions are guesswork. Next, conduct market analysis for each priority category. Understand the supply base: how many credible suppliers exist, where they are located, what their capacity is, and how they are owned. Assess the cost drivers, such as raw material prices, energy, labour, transport, import duties, and currency. Map the value chain from origin to delivery. Identify barriers to entry, such as licences, capital, or relationships. In Africa, market analysis often reveals that apparent competition is illusory because several bidders are resellers of the same manufacturer, or that a single importer controls a critical input. Understanding this before you tender prevents wasted effort and embarrassing outcomes. Then develop a category strategy. A useful framework considers the value at stake and the level of supply risk. For high value low risk categories, run competitive tenders and negotiate hard. For high value high risk categories, pursue partnerships, long term agreements, and joint value creation. For low value high risk categories, secure supply through multiple sources, buffer stock, or standardisation to reduce dependence. For low value low risk categories, simplify through catalogues, cards, or consolidated invoicing. The strategy should state objectives, sourcing approach, timeline, resource needs, and success measures. Get it approved by stakeholders so that it has organisational backing. The sourcing process itself should be rigorous and transparent. Define requirements with users, specifying outcomes rather than brand names where possible. Decide the route to market: open tender, limited tender, request for quotation, or direct negotiation with justification. Prepare a clear request for proposal that states scope, evaluation criteria, weightings, submission requirements, and timeline. Publish or invite in line with your policy and local law. Evaluate bids using a cross functional team with separate technical and commercial scoring. Conduct due diligence on shortlisted suppliers, including site visits, reference checks, financial checks, and compliance screening. Negotiate the commercial and contractual terms, aiming for total cost of ownership rather than headline price. Total cost of ownership includes purchase price, transport, duties, inventory carrying cost, quality failures, downtime, training, and end of life disposal. In African conditions, logistics and inventory costs can dwarf price differences, so model them explicitly. Implementation is where sourcing succeeds or fails. Agree an implementation plan with the supplier covering mobilisation, staffing, systems integration, pilot orders, and full rollout. Communicate the change to internal users, especially where a new supplier replaces a long standing one. Address resistance by explaining the rationale and providing support. Monitor early performance closely and hold weekly reviews during the first ninety days. Capture savings in a way that finance can verify, distinguishing between hard savings that reduce budget and soft savings that avoid cost. Category management sustains the gains. Assign a category manager who owns the strategy, the supplier relationships, the savings pipeline, and the risk profile. The category manager works with stakeholders to forecast demand, standardise specifications, and challenge unnecessary variety. Standardisation is a powerful lever in Africa because it reduces the number of spare parts, simplifies training, and lowers inventory. It also strengthens buying power by concentrating volume. The category manager should maintain a pipeline of initiatives with estimated value and timing, and report progress monthly. Stakeholder engagement is critical. Procurement cannot deliver category strategies alone. Build a network of champions in operations, engineering, finance, and legal. Involve them in strategy development and supplier selection. Share data and celebrate wins. Where stakeholders resist, understand their concerns, which may include fear of supply disruption, loss of control, or personal relationships with incumbent suppliers. Address these directly rather than dismissing them. Finally, build capability. Strategic sourcing requires skills in data analysis, market research, negotiation, contract law, and project management. Invest in training and coaching. Use simple tools first, such as spreadsheets and templates, before buying expensive software. Document lessons learned after each major sourcing project and share them across the team. Action steps: complete a spend cube for the last twelve months, select three categories for strategic sourcing, conduct market analysis for each, and draft a one page category strategy for the highest priority. In African markets, strategic sourcing is not a one off exercise; it is a continuous cycle of analysis, sourcing, implementation, and review that compounds value over time.

lessons.title: Ethical Procurement and Anti Corruption in African Supply Chains
lessons.body: Ethics in procurement is about making decisions that are fair, transparent, and consistent with the law and with the values of the organisation. In African supply chains, ethical challenges are common and sometimes subtle. They include bribery and facilitation payments, conflicts of interest, collusive bidding, nepotism, fraudulent documentation, child and forced labour, environmental damage, and the misuse of public office. Procurement professionals are often the first line of defence, and their choices determine whether the organisation is respected or exposed. This lesson provides practical guidance on building an ethical procurement system and responding to dilemmas in African contexts. Start with the legal framework. Many African countries have anti corruption legislation, public procurement acts, and sector regulations. Examples include Kenya Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, Nigeria Public Procurement Act, South Africa Public Finance Management Act and Prevention and Combating of Corrupt Activities Act, and Ghana Public Procurement Act. In addition, multinational organisations may be subject to the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the UK Bribery Act, and similar laws in the European Union and elsewhere. These laws can apply extraterritorially, meaning conduct in Africa can create liability in another jurisdiction. Know which laws apply to you and your suppliers, and seek legal advice when unsure. The most common ethical risk in procurement is bribery, including facilitation payments. A facilitation payment is a small payment to a low level official to speed up a routine action, such as clearing goods or issuing a permit. It is illegal under most anti bribery laws, even where local custom treats it as normal. The practical answer is to design processes that reduce the need for such payments: ensure documentation is complete before submission, use experienced clearing agents, budget for official fees, and escalate delays through formal channels. Where a payment is demanded, refuse, document the request, and report it. Train staff to recognise red flags, such as requests for payment to a personal account, unusually high agent fees, or demands for cash without receipt. Conflicts of interest are another frequent issue. A conflict exists when a personal interest could improperly influence a procurement decision. Examples include a buyer whose relative owns a bidding company, a manager who accepts hospitality from a supplier during a tender, or an employee who holds shares in a supplier. The remedy is disclosure and recusal. Require all staff involved in procurement to complete an annual conflict of interest declaration and to disclose new conflicts as they arise. Maintain a register and review it before tender evaluations. Where a conflict is identified, remove the person from the process and document the decision. In African contexts, family and community ties are strong, and disclosure can feel uncomfortable, so leaders must set the tone by disclosing their own interests and treating disclosure as responsible behaviour rather than an accusation. Collusive bidding, also called bid rigging, occurs when suppliers agree among themselves on prices or on who will win. Signs include identical pricing, rotating winners, unexplained withdrawals, and bids that arrive together. Combat it by keeping bidder lists confidential, avoiding unnecessary disclosure of budgets, using electronic submission where possible, and scrutinising patterns over time. Where collusion is suspected, refer to competition authorities, which exist in many African countries, including South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, and Egypt. Fraudulent documentation is common in some markets. Suppliers may present forged tax certificates, fake bank guarantees, or altered references. Verify documents directly with the issuing authority or bank. Use independent reference checks. Require original documents where feasible, and check company registration details with the relevant registry. For high value contracts, consider independent due diligence. Human rights and labour standards require attention, particularly in agriculture, mining, construction, and manufacturing. Require suppliers to prohibit child labour, forced labour, and human trafficking, and to comply with local labour law on wages, hours, and safety. Conduct audits, including unannounced visits, and require corrective action. Where serious abuses are found, be prepared to terminate. Environmental ethics matter too. Require compliance with environmental permits, proper waste management, and responsible sourcing of materials. Avoid suppliers linked to illegal logging, wildlife trafficking, or unregulated mining. Increasingly, buyers must report on supply chain sustainability, so data collection should be built into contracts. Building an ethical system requires more than a code of conduct. It requires leadership commitment, clear policies, training, safe reporting channels, and consistent consequences. Publish a supplier code of conduct and include it in contracts. Train staff and suppliers on its requirements. Provide a confidential whistleblowing channel, and protect those who report in good faith. Investigate allegations promptly and fairly. Apply sanctions consistently, regardless of the seniority or value of the supplier involved. When facing an ethical dilemma, use a simple test. Would I be comfortable if this decision were published? Does it comply with the law and our policy? Would it survive an audit? If the answer to any question is no, stop and seek advice. Document your reasoning. Ethical procurement is not only about avoiding punishment; it protects the organisation reputation, reduces legal risk, improves supplier quality, and attracts partners who value integrity. In African markets, where trust is a key business asset, ethical behaviour is a competitive advantage. Action steps: review your code of conduct and contract clauses, run a conflict of interest declaration exercise, train your team on red flags, and establish a clear reporting channel. Ethics is everyone responsibility, but procurement must lead.

lessons.title: Digital Procurement and Data in African Contexts
lessons.body: Digital procurement uses technology to automate, standardise, and analyse purchasing activities. It covers e sourcing, e tendering, purchase to pay systems, supplier portals, contract management tools, spend analytics, and increasingly artificial intelligence. In African contexts, digital procurement offers significant opportunities but also faces real constraints, including unreliable power, limited internet bandwidth, low digital literacy among some suppliers, fragmented data, and resistance to change. This lesson explains how to plan and implement digital procurement pragmatically, with a focus on data quality and practical value. Start with a clear business case. Digital procurement is not an end in itself. Define the problems you are solving. Common problems include maverick spending, slow approval cycles, poor spend visibility, lost contracts, manual invoice processing, and weak supplier performance data. Quantify the current cost of these problems, such as the staff hours spent on manual processes, the savings lost through off contract buying, or the interest cost of late payments. Then define what success looks like, with measurable targets such as reducing purchase order cycle time by fifty percent, increasing contract compliance to ninety percent, or achieving full spend visibility within twelve months. A clear business case secures funding and keeps the project focused. Next, assess your data foundations. Digital tools are only as good as the data they process. Many African organisations have supplier master data with duplicates, missing tax numbers, inconsistent names, and outdated contact details. Item data may be described in free text with no standard codes. Before or alongside any system implementation, invest in data cleansing and governance. Create a single supplier master with unique identifiers, validated tax and registration numbers, and bank details verified independently. Create a standard item catalogue for commonly purchased goods and services. Assign data owners and define rules for creating and changing records. This work is unglamorous but it determines whether analytics and automation will deliver value. Choose tools that fit your context. Enterprise resource planning systems from global vendors are powerful but can be expensive and complex. Regional and cloud based alternatives may offer better value and easier configuration. Consider modular adoption: start with e tendering or spend analytics, prove value, then expand. Ensure the tool works on low bandwidth and on mobile devices, because many suppliers and field staff rely on phones. Provide offline capability where possible. Check data residency and protection requirements under local laws. Negotiate clear service levels for uptime and support, and ensure the vendor has local presence or reliable remote support. Implementation should be phased and inclusive. Begin with a pilot in one category or one site. Involve users from procurement, finance, operations, and IT from the start. Train suppliers, especially small and medium enterprises, on how to use the portal or submit bids electronically. Provide helpdesk support during rollout. Communicate the benefits to users, such as faster approvals and less paperwork. Address resistance by listening to concerns and adapting processes where sensible. Do not simply digitise a broken process; simplify and standardise first. For example, reduce the number of approval levels before automating them. Data analytics is where digital procurement creates insight. Build dashboards that show spend by category, supplier, business unit, and country. Track savings against targets, contract compliance, supplier performance, and payment terms. Use analytics to identify maverick spending, duplicate payments, price variances, and consolidation opportunities. In African markets, analytics can also reveal currency exposure, logistics costs, and supplier concentration risk. Start with a small number of high value reports rather than a complex data warehouse. Ensure data definitions are agreed with finance so that numbers reconcile. Automate reporting where possible so that managers receive regular updates without manual effort. Artificial intelligence is beginning to play a role in procurement, including spend classification, invoice matching, demand forecasting, and supplier risk monitoring. These applications can be valuable, but they require clean data and careful governance. Be cautious about bias in algorithms and about over reliance on automated decisions in high risk categories. Keep humans in the loop for significant awards and for ethical judgements. Cyber security is a critical consideration. Procurement systems hold sensitive commercial and personal data. Implement access controls, encryption, regular backups, and incident response plans. Train staff on phishing and password hygiene. Include cyber security requirements in supplier contracts, especially for software and cloud services. Test your backups and your response plan. Finally, measure benefits and iterate. Track the metrics defined in the business case and report progress to sponsors. Celebrate quick wins to build momentum. Review the toolset annually to ensure it still meets needs and that you are not paying for unused licences. Capture lessons learned and share them across the organisation. Action steps: document your top three procurement process problems, assess your supplier and item data quality, select one pilot area for a digital tool, and define two metrics to track. Digital procurement in Africa is not about chasing the latest technology; it is about using appropriate tools to solve real problems, supported by clean data and capable people. Done well, it transforms procurement from a back office function into a strategic partner.

quiz.q: Which document formally authorizes a supplier to deliver goods or services against agreed terms?
quiz.explanation: A purchase order is the formal contract authorizing the supplier to deliver according to agreed terms.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a purchase requisition?
options: C) To request internal approval to buy goods or services
D) To receive goods into inventory
quiz.explanation: A purchase requisition is an internal document used to request authorization to procure goods or services.

quiz.q: In procurement, what does the term three-way match refer to?
options: A) Matching requisition, purchase order, and invoice
B) Matching purchase order, goods receipt, and invoice
C) Matching quotation, purchase order, and payment
D) Matching budget, forecast, and actual spend
quiz.explanation: A three-way match compares the purchase order, goods receipt, and supplier invoice before payment.

quiz.q: Which sourcing strategy involves purchasing from a single supplier for a specific category?
quiz.explanation: Single sourcing means relying on one supplier for a particular category of goods or services.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of consolidating purchases across departments?
options: A) Increased bargaining power and lower unit costs
C) Reduced need for supplier contracts
D) Elimination of inventory holding costs
quiz.explanation: Consolidation increases volume leverage, which typically improves pricing and terms.

quiz.q: Which metric measures the percentage of purchase orders delivered on time and in full?
quiz.explanation: OTIF, or on-time in-full, measures supplier delivery reliability against schedule and quantity.

quiz.q: What is a key risk of over-reliance on a single supplier?
options: C) Supply disruption if the supplier fails
D) Reduced need for quality inspections
quiz.explanation: Depending on one supplier exposes the buyer to disruptions from capacity, financial, or operational failures.

quiz.q: Which activity typically occurs during the supplier selection phase?
options: D) Evaluating bids and negotiating terms
quiz.explanation: Supplier selection involves evaluating bids, assessing capabilities, and negotiating commercial terms.
